page_contents_html:
Neuropathic pain management

Use this pathway for adults with clinically suspected or confirmed neuropathic pain managed in non-specialist care. Identify and treat the underlying cause, agree functional goals and use time-limited medicine trials with planned review.

Key prescribing principles

  • In NHS Dumfries & Galloway, the preferred formulary sequence is amitriptyline, then gabapentin, then duloxetine or pregabalin. Move to the next option when a medicine is contraindicated, not tolerated or ineffective after an adequate trial.
  • Start low, titrate gradually and change only one medicine at a time. Review pain, function, sleep, adverse effects and continued need.
  • Gabapentin and pregabalin require creatinine-clearance-based dose adjustment and carry risks of sedation, respiratory depression, dependence and withdrawal.
  • This pathway does not apply to sciatica, chronic primary pain, cancer/palliative pain or people under 18. Trigeminal neuralgia is managed separately within this pathway.

accordion_sections.heading: Primary care assessment
accordion_sections.html:
Confirm that the pain is neuropathic

Neuropathic pain is caused by a lesion or disease affecting the somatosensory nervous system. Diagnose clinically; symptom questionnaires can support but do not replace history and examination.

  • Pain follows a neuro-anatomically plausible distribution and there is a relevant disease or lesion, for example diabetes with stocking-distribution symptoms, post-herpetic neuralgia, nerve injury or entrapment, stroke or multiple sclerosis.
  • Supportive descriptors include burning, shooting, electric-shock pain, tingling, pins and needles or numbness.
  • Look for allodynia, hyperalgesia, altered pinprick or temperature sensation, numbness, weakness, reflex change, autonomic change or skin/trophic change.
  • If the neuropathic component remains uncertain, use the full DN4 screening questionnaire below.

Preferred screening aid: DN4

The DN4 is the preferred tool because it combines symptom descriptors with a brief bedside sensory examination. It supports clinical assessment but does not make the diagnosis on its own.

  1. Ask about 7 features: burning, painful cold, electric shocks, tingling, pins and needles, numbness and itching.
  2. Examine for 3 findings: reduced sensation to light touch, reduced sensation to pinprick, and pain caused or increased by light brushing.
  3. Score: award 1 point for each feature present, giving a total of 0-10. A score of 4 or more supports a neuropathic component. A lower score does not exclude neuropathic pain.

Interpret the score alongside a neuro-anatomically plausible pain distribution, evidence of a relevant lesion or disease, and the focused neurological examination. Do not use DN4 alone to label widespread, nociplastic or chronic primary pain as neuropathic. Use the full DN4 questionnaire to record the assessment.

Assess cause, impact and risk

  • Record onset, duration, distribution, severity, sleep disturbance and effect on mobility, mood, work, relationships and daily activities.
  • Identify the underlying cause and whether it is stable or deteriorating. Treat reversible causes where possible.
  • Review renal and hepatic function, cardiovascular disease, falls risk, frailty, pregnancy potential, mental health, alcohol or substance use and all concurrent medicines.
  • Check for opioids, benzodiazepines, Z-drugs, sedating antihistamines and other CNS depressants before considering a gabapentinoid.
  • Investigations should follow the presentation and suspected cause. For unexplained peripheral neuropathy consider FBC, U&E, LFT, HbA1c, B12/folate, TFT and serum protein electrophoresis, with further investigation or referral guided by findings.

Use the correct pathway

  • Sciatica: do not start gabapentin, pregabalin or another antiepileptic for sciatica. Use the current spinal/sciatica pathway.
  • Chronic primary pain: do not initiate a gabapentinoid solely for chronic primary pain. Use the chronic pain pathway and shared decision-making guidance.
  • Cancer or palliative pain: use the relevant oncology or Scottish Palliative Care guidance and seek specialist advice early.
  • Under 18: seek paediatric or condition-specific advice.

accordion_sections.heading: Treatment principles and review
accordion_sections.html:
Agree the treatment goal

Explain that complete pain relief is uncommon. Agree a meaningful goal such as improved sleep, walking, self-care, work or participation. Record a baseline pain score and one or more functional measures so benefit can be judged.

Offer non-pharmacological management to everyone

  • Explain the diagnosis and address fear of movement or tissue damage where appropriate.
  • Encourage pacing, graded activity, sleep support and maintenance of valued activity.
  • Consider physiotherapy, occupational therapy, psychological approaches or condition-specific rehabilitation.
  • Signpost to NHS Inform chronic pain, Pain Association Scotland, Pain Concern and the Right Decisions chronic pain shared decision aid.

Safe medicine trials

  • Discuss expected benefit, common adverse effects, driving and work safety, titration, withdrawal and what will happen if the treatment does not help.
  • Start one medicine at a time. Review early after starting or changing treatment to assess titration, tolerability and adverse effects.
  • At each review assess pain, function, sleep, physical and psychological wellbeing, adverse effects, adherence and continued need.
  • If there is no worthwhile benefit after an adequate trial at the maximum tolerated dose, taper and stop, then offer the next suitable option.
  • Continue an existing treatment that is clearly effective and tolerated, with regular review.

Gabapentinoid safety

Gabapentin and pregabalin are Schedule 3 controlled drugs. Discuss addiction, dependence, tolerance and withdrawal before prescribing. Risk is higher with current or previous substance misuse or mental health disorder, but can occur at therapeutic doses and with short-term use.

Use particular caution in older or frail people, renal impairment, respiratory or neurological disease, and with opioids, benzodiazepines, Z-drugs, alcohol or other CNS depressants. Sedation and respiratory depression can be fatal. Use the lowest effective dose and provide a clear review and stopping plan.

accordion_sections.heading: Stepwise pharmacological treatment
accordion_sections.html:
Follow the NHS D&G preferred formulary sequence below. Skip to the next option when a medicine is contraindicated or unsuitable. NICE permits amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin or pregabalin as initial treatment, so individual patient factors and informed preference remain important.

Step 1 - amitriptyline

  • Start 10 mg at night, taken 1-2 hours before bed. Increase by 10 mg every 1-2 weeks according to benefit and tolerability.
  • The usual effective neuropathic-pain dose is 25-75 mg daily. Use the lowest effective dose. Seek specialist or experienced prescribing advice before considering a dose above 75 mg.
  • Analgesic benefit is usually apparent within 2-4 weeks of reaching an effective dose. Do not continue escalation when adverse effects outweigh benefit.
  • Common limiting effects include sedation, dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, confusion, urinary retention, falls and postural hypotension.
  • Avoid or seek advice with recent myocardial infarction, significant arrhythmia or conduction disease, narrow-angle glaucoma, urinary retention/prostatism, high anticholinergic burden or substantial overdose risk.
  • If morning sedation occurs, move the dose earlier in the evening. If it persists, switch to another formulary option; confirm the local position before using nortriptyline for pain.

Step 2 - gabapentin

  • Start 300 mg at night. In older, frail or medicine-sensitive patients start 100 mg at night.
  • Increase weekly to 300 mg twice daily and then 300 mg three times daily. Thereafter titrate gradually according to response, adverse effects and creatinine clearance.
  • Where tolerated, an adequate local formulary trial will usually require at least 1200 mg/day. The licensed maximum for peripheral neuropathic pain is 3600 mg/day, but do not escalate without evidence of additional benefit.
  • Consider asymmetrical dosing with the larger dose in the evening when daytime sedation limits treatment.
  • Reduce the dose in renal impairment. Stop titration when the agreed goal is achieved or adverse effects become unacceptable.

Step 3 - duloxetine or pregabalin

Choose according to the cause of pain, comorbidity, concurrent medicines, renal function, adverse-effect profile and patient preference.

Duloxetine

  • Duloxetine is licensed for diabetic peripheral neuropathic pain. The recommended dose is 60 mg once daily. A preliminary 30 mg once-daily step may be used for tolerability where clinically appropriate.
  • Evaluate response by 8 weeks and stop if ineffective. Reassess benefit and ongoing need at least every 3 months.
  • Some patients who partially respond to 60 mg may benefit from a higher dose; review the risk-benefit balance carefully and do not exceed 120 mg/day in divided doses.
  • Do not use with creatinine clearance below 30 mL/min, hepatic impairment or uncontrolled hypertension. Check interactions and serotonergic burden.
  • Avoid co-prescribing with tramadol or tapentadol unless explicitly directed by a specialist because of serotonin and CNS toxicity.

Pregabalin

  • Start 50 mg twice daily; consider 25 mg twice daily in older, frail or medicine-sensitive patients.
  • Increase the total daily dose by 25-50 mg each week according to response and tolerability. The usual effective range is 150-600 mg/day in 2 or 3 divided doses.
  • Reduce the dose and adjust frequency according to creatinine clearance. Do not continue escalation without meaningful additional benefit.
  • Apply the gabapentinoid safety warning above. Pregabalin above 300 mg/day with an opioid is particularly associated with increased opioid-related death.

Medicines not to start routinely

Do not initiate long-term tramadol, morphine, cannabis extract, capsaicin 8% patch, lacosamide, lamotrigine, levetiracetam, oxcarbazepine, topiramate, venlafaxine or valproate for neuropathic pain in non-specialist care unless advised by a specialist. Tramadol should be considered only as short-term rescue therapy when clinically necessary.

accordion_sections.heading: Localised pain and trigeminal neuralgia
accordion_sections.html:
Localised neuropathic pain

  • Capsaicin 0.075% cream: consider when pain is localised and the patient wishes to avoid, or cannot tolerate, oral treatment. Apply a small amount 3-4 times daily for 6-8 weeks, then review. Warn that local burning is common and avoid broken skin and mucous membranes.
  • Lidocaine 5% plaster: licensed for post-herpetic neuralgia. Do not use routinely for other indications; follow the local formulary or seek Pain Team/MDT advice.
  • Capsaicin 8% patch (Qutenza): specialist treatment only.

Trigeminal neuralgia

Offer carbamazepine as initial treatment. Confirm that the presentation is consistent with trigeminal neuralgia and exclude dental, ophthalmic or other secondary causes where indicated.

  • Start 100 mg twice daily and titrate slowly in steps of 100-200 mg every 2 weeks according to response and tolerability. Do not exceed 1600 mg/day.
  • Before starting check weight/BMI, FBC, LFT, U&E and sodium; consider renal function and ECG where indicated. Check interactions and pregnancy risk. Follow current HLA-B*1502 testing advice for people with relevant Asian ancestry.
  • Monitor according to current SPS/BNF advice and counsel about rash, fever, mouth ulcers, bruising, jaundice and hyponatraemia symptoms.
  • If carbamazepine is contraindicated, ineffective or not tolerated, seek expert advice and consider early condition-specific or specialist pain referral. Do not initiate another medicine for trigeminal neuralgia without specialist advice.

accordion_sections.heading: Renal dosing, switching and withdrawal
accordion_sections.html:
Use creatinine clearance

Base gabapentin and pregabalin dosing on creatinine clearance, not unadjusted eGFR. Use the current BNF, product information and an approved creatinine-clearance calculator. Recalculate after a material change in renal function or body weight.

Gabapentin total daily dose by creatinine clearance

CrCl (mL/min)Total daily dose
80 or above900-3600 mg/day in divided doses
50-79600-1800 mg/day in divided doses
30-49300-900 mg/day in divided doses
15-29150-600 mg/day; 150 mg may be given as 300 mg on alternate days
Below 15150-300 mg/day; reduce proportionately at very low CrCl

Pregabalin total daily dose by creatinine clearance

The table shows product-information starting doses. The lower 50 mg twice-daily local starting dose above may be used to improve tolerability before titrating towards the dose appropriate for renal function.

CrCl (mL/min)Product-information starting doseMaximum doseFrequency
60 or above150 mg/day600 mg/day2 or 3 divided doses
30-5975 mg/day300 mg/day2 or 3 divided doses
15-2925-50 mg/day150 mg/dayOnce daily or twice daily
Below 1525 mg/day75 mg/dayOnce daily

Haemodialysis requires supplementary dosing: check current BNF/product information or seek pharmacy advice.

Switching gabapentin and pregabalin

Do not prescribe them together as long-term combination therapy. If switching is appropriate, use the current NHS SPS gabapentin-pregabalin switching guidance. Direct switch, short cross-taper or taper-and-switch may be used; choose according to clinical risk. Account for renal function, respiratory risk and additive effects during any overlap.

Withdrawal

Do not stop amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin or pregabalin abruptly after regular use. Agree an individual taper. The schedules below are practical starting examples from the local draft; use smaller reductions and longer intervals if withdrawal symptoms occur. Tapering may take weeks or months.

MedicineSuggested initial reduction
Amitriptyline / nortriptylineReduce by 10 mg each week
Gabapentin above 900 mg/dayReduce total daily dose by 300 mg each week
Gabapentin 900 mg/day or lessReduce total daily dose by 100 mg each week
PregabalinReduce total daily dose by 25-50 mg each week
DuloxetineReduce by 30 mg each week

If intolerable symptoms develop, pause the taper or return to the previous tolerated dose, then resume more slowly. Seek specialist or pharmacy advice for high doses, long treatment duration, severe withdrawal, coexisting epilepsy or suspected dependence.

accordion_sections.heading: Who to refer and how urgently
accordion_sections.html:
Emergency or same-day assessment

Use the relevant acute pathway rather than a routine Pain Service referral for:

  • Suspected cauda equina syndrome or spinal cord compression
  • New or rapidly progressive motor weakness, major gait deterioration, bulbar or respiratory dysfunction
  • Suspected spinal infection, malignancy, fracture or another acute structural cause
  • Severe medicine toxicity, respiratory depression, serotonin syndrome, serious rash or acute suicidality

Early condition-specific or specialist advice

  • Diagnostic uncertainty, unexplained or rapidly progressive neuropathy, prominent motor or autonomic features, cranial neuropathy or abnormal investigations
  • Underlying neurological, oncological, infectious, vascular or compressive condition is deteriorating
  • Suspected complex regional pain syndrome - arrange early rehabilitation/condition-specific input; do not wait for multiple medicine failures
  • Trigeminal neuralgia when carbamazepine is contraindicated, ineffective or not tolerated
  • Pregnancy, breastfeeding or complex polypharmacy where medicine selection is uncertain

Refer to the specialist Pain Service

  • Severe pain or pain that substantially limits sleep, mobility, self-care, work or participation
  • Persistent neuropathic pain despite adequate, documented trials of suitable local formulary options at the maximum tolerated dose
  • Unacceptable adverse effects or complex dependence/withdrawal preventing safe optimisation
  • Consideration of Qutenza, interventional treatment or multidisciplinary pain assessment and rehabilitation
  • The patient requests specialist review after an informed discussion of what the service can offer

Include in the referral

  • Working diagnosis, suspected cause, duration and neuro-anatomical distribution
  • Relevant neurological examination, red-flag assessment, investigations and condition-specific treatment
  • Pain, sleep and functional impact, psychological and social factors, and agreed goals
  • Every medicine tried: maximum dose, duration, benefit, adverse effects and withdrawal outcome
  • Renal function, relevant comorbidities, concurrent sedatives/opioids and substance-use history
  • Self-management, rehabilitation and community services already tried

accordion_sections.heading: Who not to refer
accordion_sections.html:
Continue management in primary care when the diagnosis and cause are clear, there are no red flags or progressive neurological features, and pain is stable or improving with self-management and a tolerated medicine.

Routine Pain Service referral is usually unnecessary when:

  • The patient is benefiting from a safe, stable treatment with planned review
  • A reversible cause has not yet been investigated or treated
  • Suitable formulary treatments have not yet had an adequate titration and review, unless pain is severe or function is substantially impaired
  • The main need is diagnosis or treatment of a neurological, spinal, vascular, cancer, infection, headache, dental or mental health condition - use the relevant condition-specific service
  • The presentation is sciatica or chronic primary pain and the appropriate pathway has not yet been followed

Do not refer solely to obtain continuation of an ineffective high-dose medicine. Review benefit and harm, then agree a supported taper where appropriate.
